text:
**UPDATE: My review below still stands since they have done nothing to improve this app, but recently they have moved to payments outside of the App Store, which is very shady because they make it difficult for you to find and cancel the subscriptions. If you sign up for anything, they automatically subscribe you now. Stay away from this app.**


Bumble is an extremely frustrating app. They update it constantly, but the only change they seem to make is the constant tweak to the font size, placement, or highlight colors. The core experience has not changed.  


The biggest problem with Bumble is that, unlike most dating apps, they base dating location entirely on your current location, not your "lives in" location. This makes it particularly annoying when you are away from home (the travel mode feature is a joke), and it makes it very annoying for matching. Only hookup apps work this way, and they insist this is a serious dating app. This is a big problem for me because a major airport is within my search radius so 50% of my matches are women at the airport who live hundreds or thousands of miles away. There is no way to exclude locations.


Having to scroll to the bottom to see where the person is currently location and lives (if they choose to fill this in since it's optional) is incredibly annoying. All other dating apps, even hookup apps, have it at the top. Bumble makes me waste time reading a profile and scrolling only to find out they live half way across the country. Scrolling also means accidentally clicking Super Swipes, since it's so easy to hit this. At least once a week at least one Super Swipe is a mistake. There's no way to cancel this or request credit. 


Another major problem with the app is their filters. They force you to pay for these, but they don't work very well. The filter only includes people who answer exactly what you choose. The vast majority of profiles don't bother to fill out half the information since it's all optional. Their filters aren't smart enough to include an option for no response, so I can't include them in my search.


Lastly, for the spotlight searches, stop showing me people that live hundreds of miles away. Respect my dating preferences. I am not interested in dating someone on the other side of the country.

text:
As a gay man, I’ve been using Bumble since it first opened its platform to the LGBTQIA+ community, and watching this app deteriorate over the years has been genuinely embarrassing. What was once a usable dating platform has turned into a broken, overpriced mess filled with fake profiles, nonsensical algorithms, and a complete disregard for user experience. At this point, the app is bordering on unusable.
First, the location and matching system are absolutely absurd. I live in NYC, one of the largest, most densely populated cities in the world, yet Bumble somehow insists on showing me potential matches from upstate New York, rural New England, and even Canada. When I narrow the distance settings to reflect my actual area, I’m met with the laughable claim that there are “no more potential matches nearby.” That is objectively ridiculous. There is simply no believable explanation for an app operating in New York City to pretend there are no gay men within a reasonable radius unless the algorithm is fundamentally broken or the platform is artificially withholding profiles to manipulate engagement.
What makes this even worse is that the only way to see additional people is to expand the radius to 100+ miles, which completely defeats the purpose of location-based dating. Nobody living in Manhattan or Brooklyn should have to search halfway into another state just to find active profiles. The entire system feels either incompetently designed or intentionally manipulative.
The second issue and honestly the more disgraceful one is the overwhelming infestation of AI bots, scammers, and fake accounts. The sheer volume of fraudulent profiles on Bumble is impossible to ignore. At this point, it feels less like a dating app and more like a poorly moderated spam network. A shocking percentage of profiles are obviously fake: stolen photos, incoherent bios, robotic prompt answers, and accounts that cannot even form complete sentences. It is painfully obvious that little to no meaningful moderation is taking place.
There is absolutely no excuse for swiping through 10 profiles and finding that more than half are clearly fabricated. The fact that Bumble continues charging outrageously high weekly subscription fees while failing to maintain even the most basic level of authenticity or quality control is insulting to paying users. You are asking people to spend real money on a platform where a substantial portion of the user base appears to be fake, inactive, or algorithmically recycled.
At this point, Bumble feels less interested in helping people connect and more interested in inflating engagement metrics while delivering an increasingly hollow product. For a company that markets itself as progressive and community-oriented, the actual user experience especially for LGBTQIA+ users has become frustrating, deceptive, and deeply disappointing.

text:
I wanted to give an honest account of my experience using Bumble, along with patterns I’ve consistently seen across people I’ve met and conversations with fellow Bumble users.


Longevity on the app-
One of the first things that stood out: a surprising number of users have been on the app for years, often 4 to 8. That raises a legitimate question about the product’s effectiveness. If the goal is to help people form meaningful connections, that kind of tenure suggests something isn’t working.


Pricing and monetization-
The premium experience feels misaligned with the value delivered. Features range from around $1.99+ for highlights to $40+ bundles for SuperSwipes, Highlights or Notes, with pricing incentives to buy more at once. In theory, more spend should improve visibility, but in practice, it feels like a high input, low return system. Paying for these features rarely leads to meaningful engagement, and the structure encourages continued spending without a clear improvement in outcomes. At a certain point, it starts to feel less like a dating platform and more like a slot machine… and you’d likely have better odds in Vegas, not just winning, but actually meeting someone.


Match volume vs. meaningful interaction-
You can match with a wide range of people, anywhere from dozens to thousands, but volume doesn’t translate into quality. Even with paid features, engagement is low. A SuperSwipe or note often results in minimal effort responses, like “hey,” if any response at all. The core issue seems to be attention fragmentation. People aren’t just juggling conversations within the app, but also outside of it, while continuing to swipe through hundreds of profiles. Any single interaction becomes low priority.


Filtering and product design-
The filtering system is where the experience breaks down further. In theory, filters should narrow your pool to people who meet your criteria. In practice, applying them can reduce hundreds of potential matches down to a dozen or so. That forces you to widen filters you don’t actually want, either because many users don’t fully complete their profiles, or because the system doesn’t reliably enforce those preferences.


The result is a time consuming loop: swipe through large volumes, manually filter in your head, and repeat. Whether by design or limitation, the platform seems to prioritize keeping a broad pool over delivering precise matches. Over time, it can feel like matches are surfaced slowly, sometimes only a handful per month, which may help explain why so many users remain on the app for years rather than finding someone within a shorter timeframe.


Culture and user behavior-
Over time, the platform starts to feel increasingly transactional. A noticeable number of profiles explicitly say things like “here to date with intention,” which ironically highlights how much misalignment and mixed intent exists on the app.


There’s also a recurring theme of people trying to get off the app as quickly as possible, often stated directly in bios: “please get me off this app,” “let’s get off here,” or “let’s meet so we can get off the app.” It creates a dynamic where users don’t seem invested in the platform itself, but are instead trying to bypass it.


More broadly, the experience suggests a misalignment between user goals and product outcomes. Instead of efficiently matching people, the design often keeps users in a prolonged cycle of swiping, matching, and low quality interactions. The end result is an environment that is difficult to take seriously if you’re looking for something meaningful, arguably even more transactional than platforms like Tinder. From a user’s perspective, it can feel less like a product optimized for helping people find love and more like one optimized for keeping them there and not finding it.


Bottom line-
At this point, the return on time, energy, and money doesn’t justify continued use. More importantly, there’s a consistent pattern I’ve noticed, people on the app are genuinely unhappy, and they say it openly when you ask about their experience. That alone is enough to question the environment.


At a certain point, the tradeoff becomes clear. Endless swiping, surface level messaging, and continued spending lead to diminishing returns, both emotionally and practically. 


In contrast, real life interactions, while less frequent, tend to be more grounded, more intentional, and ultimately more worth pursuing.

text:
I ran an experiment with the three big dating apps. I paid for one month of each subscription and compared the results. Bumble gave me zero success. The dating pool is much smaller too. I had to increase my radius after running out of options pretty quickly; which is saying something considering I live in one of the biggest cities in the US. Your experience might be different but from the looks of recent reviews I doubt that’s the case.


You pay for extra features like super likes and spotlights each week but they don’t roll over. If I’m paying for features they should stay there. I regularly get matches on the other two apps and even consistently using Bumble I got one match that was a person I am *positive* I didn’t swipe right on. This leads me to believe they’re matching you with bots to keep engagement. Don’t waste your time on the free version and definitely do not pay for it either.
